title: Assistant GM Dave Sears Press Conference 8.17.26 | AZ Cardinals
text: Dave, this time of year, and and obviously like you just had it, you guys had it with Chase, like what goes into the process of a significant piece getting hurt and then trying to figure out, okay, we we want to go get a veteran, we've got the guys already on the thing, you know, we were going to wait. Like how how do how does that process kind of >> Uh it's probably different for every player that gets hurt in a situation like Chase. Unfortunate, but that happens every year. So, we're well into the preseason scouting process, you know, right now we're all kind of in a little uh preseason scouting coma, you know what I mean? As soon as these games start going in, all you're doing is watching games, watching players, uh getting what's called your ready list or your emergency list. We're not at that point yet because we're still in competition for our own roster, so is every other team. Um usually they're going to wait a little bit to start making moves, things like that. You'll see guys come across the waiver. Um but we're probably a couple weeks out from people really starting to make moves in that sense. Um but it's really still internal competition, you know, we've got some good depth guys on this roster right now who are fighting for spots. Uh obviously Chase's role was undefined at this point. He's a rookie, he's still trying to, you know, find his way. Um just an unfortunate situation with him, but I think that roster churning process, looking at depth, regardless of it's if it's, you know, a depth swing guy, a starting-level player, you're always in the kind of same mode of who's out there, who's available, who can we get to upgrade our roster. >> So, how much is your kind of day-to-day um now split between watching tape of your own roster and practice and and preseason and making those decisions versus, as you said, watching other teams and and looking for who could become available on the field? >> I don't know if it's split, but it's all crammed in there in one form or fashion, you know? I'd say I don't split much sleep involved in it, you know what I mean? Like we're That's really all we're doing right now is just watching tape. Watch tape, watch in practice, watch in tape, watch in practice. That's scouts across the league, that's all we're doing, you know what I mean? >> that change when you go into the regular season? Like what does your day-to-day kind of change into? >> Well, the practice tape is a little different, you know what I mean? Once you're you're not in full pads, the practices aren't I won't say not competitive, but it's a different level. You know, there's more I haven't been through a regular season yet with coach LaFleur, obviously, but more walk-through, more jog-through where you're not evaluating competitive portion. So, it's not and you're not in the can this guy make the roster team, you know, trying to whittle down a roster from 90 to 53. You're just trying to see like how do some guys look? How do these um practice squad guys look? Are these guys improving? Those level players more so than you're evaluating maybe your starting level players or guys fighting for the next spot cuz you're not in that same level of competition at that point. >> When you guys do whittle down the roster, what's the I wouldn't say percentage, but like obviously there's the personnel side, you Monty and your group, and then there's the coaching side. Like how does that discussion go? Does it Does it start with Monty and okay, we got to be looking at what these contracts look like or whatever or does it start with the coaches and then you play off of that? >> I think it's all collaborative. I mean, it's really Mike and Monty making the final decisions with input from both sides, I would say. I mean, the coaches are busy coaching all these guys and they certainly have input on how they are day-to-day in the room, how they're picking up the schemes, how they're performing, executing the X's and O's to a different level than the scouts' perception. And the scouts are looking at, you know, how are they performing to their eye on the tape and this is what we think the pecking order is. There's probably less conflict or disagreement than you might think. I mean, most of the time it's synced up pretty good. And then when it's not, you know, Monty and Michael resolve that. >> How How different I know that they the last couple three years, whatever it was, they they kind of shifted you guys were making those final cuts in the middle of the week and they they shifted it back to Sunday and I don't know if that's earlier or later. How does that change? >> it's a little earlier in the week. I think it was Tuesday, if I'm right. I don't think it really changes cuz once camp starts like days mean nothing. Like I don't know what day it is. You you honestly, it's just the next day and all that kind of stuff. So, you play your last game, you're ready to make your cuts, you're ready to make your claims, all that kind of stuff, set your practice squad. So, I don't think it really matters what day of the week it is, per se. >> It feels like the wide receivers room is just top to bottom been really competitive. Just what's been your take on it throughout >> Yeah, I think I think that's accurate. I think it's This is one of the deeper I don't know, what do we have? 11, you know, whatever it is, one through 11 guys, like where everybody's fairly competitive. There's not a couple guys at the bottom where you're just like, okay, these guys are out of here the first chance we get, type thing. Like all these guys are playing really well. I'm not saying they're all at the same level, but for the roles, I think it's a really competitive room. It's been fun to watch some of the younger guys competing, making plays in practice. So, yeah, it's been exciting to see those guys. >> When you're making those cuts down to 53, how how do you kind of balance what a guy has maybe shown you in camp versus, you know, a guy who who maybe when you were scouting him in the draft, you saw a higher talent level? Like how how do you kind of balance your prior assessments from years past versus what you've seen now? >> You know, that's always kind of the What is this guy's ceiling? Is he going to hit it? You know, how long can we wait on him to actually start producing? But I think it's the guys that can carry practice into the preseason for that level lower level of of player that you're talking about. You know, practice is great. It's different than the games. You know what I mean? Preseason games are great. They're different from regular season. Regular season is great. It's different from the postseason. Like there's always these steps up that you want to see a guy make the next step. So, I think you want to see him do it in practice, but then you really need to see him do it in the game if he's got the opportunity. Some of these guys don't get the same opportunities in the game and it's harder to evaluate, especially when you're doing all these preseason games. Like a guy may come available that had very little production in the preseason, but scouts who liked this guy in the draft and you'll see a team claim him even though he didn't have much preseason production. Well, that's because what they thought of him for the most part going into the draft or something like that. >> On that note, the running backs room is has a lot of players and some returners. The special teams comes into play there. How do you overcome the challenges from an evaluation standpoint when you have players like James who you know and and Trey who showed you some things who are not able to physically participate right now? >> Yeah, and and that's tough because um you can count on guys, but it's hard to count on guys who aren't playing, aren't practicing. And then when are they going to be back? When are they going to be available versus what do we have in the room now versus uh how many players do we have to keep at some other position that's starting to perform well or they're getting hit by the injury bug so you need to keep extra guys there. Um and it's that's the puzzle of the final 53 type thing. And while our running back room is really deep on paper, you know, we got multiple guys out right now. It's not as deep at practice. That that kind of thing. So um that that is a little bit of a dilemma, you know I mean, but once they put things on tape like James for his entire career, you can pretty much count on when James Conner's out there, he's going to be a good player. It's just a question of when he's going to be back out there, you know, and that's for James and Drew and Monte Mike to figure it out, you know. >> From a workload and responsibilities standpoint, how is your department or how how was it impacted by the Ryan Shazier situation happening so close to camp? >> Uh not you know, honestly, I'm not going to get too much into that cuz I don't have a lot of information. To your direct question, we have plenty of people to fill in for the roles that we're missing right now, myself included. We've had multiple people with experience as college directors. Uh we just promoted Vance to uh Alphonso Allen to assistant college director so he's taking on a lot of that role on. So, you know, it's all hands on deck and and we're absorbing it, you know what I mean? >> How would you assess just Marvin Harris and just from when you got here to where it is right now? >> Um I think, you know, Marvin's a good player. He's always been a good player. I think Marvin's releases and routes are are really good. I think Marvin's, like any young player, uh I think every year there's something that's improving in his game. I think Marv's a technically sound player, and I think you'll see an improvement in Marv's game this year. I think the offense suits Marv well, and I think um he's been really productive in practice this so far. You know, he had the great touchdown catch in the game the other day. We've seen catches like that uh pretty commonplace in practice every day, so. >> When you just watch Carson Beck in practice and then Cam, where do you see kind of all his experience in college kind of paying off now? >> Um I mean, I don't I don't think we've seen the guy get rattled. I think that's something that I could say. Um in the preseason game, you don't see a lot of stuff being thrown at this guy. I mean, that's pretty universal across the league. If you look at the quarterback rookie quarterbacks that played in the preseason, I think the you know, you had [snorts] a bunch of guys over 70% completion. I think across the board every rookie it was like 65% completion with a ton of touchdowns versus So, like that is not realistic of what they're all going to do going forward, but I think with Carson it you know, he's not a developmental player from a hasn't been on the field standpoint. So, playing in an environment like that, he was not overwhelmed. He was not, you know, confused. He's just looks like a relaxed player playing football. You know, he played well in that situation. >> I know obviously he hasn't coached a a real game yet where you're doing a proper game plan and everything, but what have been your early impressions of what Mike has brought to the organization? Like >> Uh yeah, I mean, I think the guy's got tremendous energy, tremendous knowledge. He comes from a coaching family. You know, the guy's born to be a football coach. Um what it was always impressive in the interview process and through this point is he's in total command of the room. Uh you can talk to him about anything football related, whether that be, you know, scouting players to coaching offense, coaching defense, coaching special teams. He's got a grasp of all of it, and he's really natural in front of the team and anytime he's talking football. So, there's never a question of if the guy's BSing or not. I mean, the guy knows his I think that's obvious. >> Do you remember what your evaluation of Michael Wilson was when he was competing for the three? >> Uh yeah. I mean, Mike Mike's a good player. He's got a twitch off the ball. He's got really good releases. Um you know, he's a good route runner. He's got good hands. He's powerfully built. I mean, you can obviously see that. He's really gritty guy. He's got instincts. I mean, there's not a lot of negatives to Mike's game. We all like Mike. He's a good player. He's a hell of a blocker. You know, I don't have many negative things to say about Mike. >> Did you see a thousand yards out of him back then? >> I don't think of it in terms like that. I mean, I see a guy who can get open and catch the ball. >> Cornerback is a position that you guys have really focused on the draft the last couple years. You know, Ronald Johnson, Denzel Burke going into year two. Not to put them into a box, but big picture, where do you typically see the biggest jump player development-wise from a cornerback from year one to year two? you know, like like any young player, I think it's just the game slows down a little bit for them because they're in a routine. They figured out how to manage their body. They figured out how to manage their off time. They figured out how to, you know, work the weight room into it. The the rehab therapy. Like they have a routine. When you're a rookie, and you see that with a lot of rookies and, you know, dealing with what would they're dealing with, they don't really have time to establish that routine. You know, they're coming right from an All-Star game to, you know, whether it's playoffs, combine, pro day, into the OTAs, whatever, um trying to figure out where to live, where to eat, all this kind of stuff. And so, it's not till year two, and I think across a guy middle OTAs next year, hey, how do you feel now compared to your rookie year? They're all going to tell you, I feel great. I'm in the best shape of my life. I feel so much stronger. You know, it's cuz they find the routine. So, I think corners specifically, probably technique-wise, you know, probably technique-wise, whether that's, you know, your press technique, your off technique, whatever, just the understanding of what offenses are doing, the amount of time they have to study the game now versus maybe when they're in college. Um but I think really kind of technique-wise, I don't think guys get tremendously faster or looser or anything like that. But that part of it, the mental side. >> What is the key for Will Johnson to kind of reach the ceiling that that you guys obviously saw in the draft? >> Cuz like I feel like he had a he had a really good rookie season, but not quite at that elite level that that a lot of people kind of saw as his ceiling. >> Yeah, I don't I mean, I think like everybody else, he's going to continue to improve as long as he continues doing all the right things, which is, you know, a lot of things I just mentioned. So, um, I can't I don't like to put ceilings on guys, but Will's a good player. He can be a very good player, and I think he'll continue to, you know, there's nothing Will's not doing, you know what I mean? Will works his ass off, he studies, he's smart, you know, he trains right. Will's been, um, you know, out there every day working. >> And there's probably a method to the madness in terms of preseason snap counts and playing time and all that stuff. Whenever Whenever Whenever you do have injuries to guys like Jeremiah and Chase, does that change your guys' mindset at all, or do you guys kind of trust the process whenever it comes to that? >> In terms of snap counts? >> In terms of how much you think a guy's going to play, and then maybe do you let the injuries impact that at all? >> I really don't have anything to do with how much a guy plays or doesn't play, so that's more of a coach LaFleur question. >> Thanks, David. >> Appreciate it. Thank you.

title: Zaven Collins Press Conference 8.16.26 | AZ Cardinals
text: I mean, I know you guys didn't get a lot of run the other day, but how did you feel like the unit >> It was good. Uh going back to watching film of some of the guys. I mean, it's always nice to see um some new stuff. Obviously, the offense coordinator came or the guy calling plays comes from Seattle. So, it's nothing that we weren't um uh used to. Uh so, definitely had some things that we kind of thought they were going to do and just kind of, you know, it's preseason, but uh yeah, I thought it was good. Some minor mistakes [clears throat] and some stuff that we had to fix, but it was good overall. >> You've talked before about all the different ways you've been used within this defense, and Mike was talking about how uh you could have seven different pitches, but sometimes it's best to just throw the fastball and come off the edge. Do you feel like you've been afforded the opportunity to come off the edge a lot more at this camp? >> Uh yeah, I mean, we've uh done some things. Uh I wouldn't say it was definitely dialed back from it has been in the past as far as like all the different things that I do. But yeah, there's some some stuff to make it simple and just have less rules and just go, and it's it's nice. Um you know, just being able to go downhill, and uh obviously, there's some hard downs where I'm asked to do some certain things, but yeah, for sure. >> How's it been getting to know Dewey and just playing with him? >> Oh, I love Dewey. Dewey's awesome. I love Dewey. He's He's He's hilarious. We talk all the time. Um we talk about golf. We talk about all kinds of other stuff. You know, he I think he lives in Colorado still, so talk about him being there and his experience and, you know, uh him being in Jacksonville and, you know, he played with Dennis and stuff. So, uh yeah, we we talk quite a bit, and uh he's a great player, great guy. He's uh you know, got a great knowledge for the game, and you know, try and pick his brain about stuff when I can. >> With uh with him being from Colorado, is he outdoorsy like you are? >> Uh yeah, I I mean, in the sense of like he likes to golf and stuff. So, yeah, I'm not sure if he's like out in the middle of the mountains and stuff. I'm sure he is, you know. There's definitely a huge aspect there for them. But yeah, definitely. >> With the hair flowing, do you ever do a double take of thinking it's dead? >> Oh yeah, for sure. I was like, I wonder what the dynamic was cuz usually there's only about one of those guys on a team. And I was like, they definitely had two, so that's a different a different change up. So yeah, I think it's hilarious. >> We've seen a lot of Eku start to do some get some run with the ones. What have you seen from him as he's developed from last year into this year? >> Yeah, I think obviously him coming in and having a full off-season and being able to learn and understand how the defense works. Him understanding what they want from him and just being able to go and do what he does. He has a you know, he has a unique skill set in how he rushes the passer and how he does in the run game and pass game. So him getting the full OTA, full camp and him being able to go do that has been awesome. He's really gets he gets off the ball really well, too. So he's he's done well. >> Hey Zach, what is what makes a good run defense? Is it a mentality? Is it the execution? >> I think there's a little bit of both there, right? You know, you definitely you want to be sound in the scheme, but sometimes you know, you don't want to call it fit ball. Not you know what I mean? So sometimes there's guys whenever yeah, they kind of got us on a play, but if someone goes and you know, takes out two offensive players and a you know, we call it change the math. You change the math there, that's that play is ruined. We talk about that quite a bit quite a bit. You know, this isn't fit ball. It's be a fit ball. See the ball, hit the ball, take out two guys, get rid of your guy, get to the ball as fast as you can, especially on the edge. You know, when they got tight ends, certain people blocking us. Got to be able to go do that. And same thing goes for D-linemen and linebackers and uh Nick really really emphasizes that to us and so does Feeney about you know, this is what you don't just take one for one. You got to get off of that block and go get to the ball. Especially when it's in the adjacent gap. >> Last year, Colaeus was a guy who changed the math on a lot of run plays. Who do you think on this kind of upfront uh in the unit group this year can can be that player who's changing the math? >> So far it's been Big Bill. >> [laughter] >> I mean, he's tore it up. He's done well. Um you know, I think uh there is there's a bunch of guys. Uh Walt's done really well in the run game, I think. Um he's had some really good flashes uh on the practice practice tape. Um Roy's always been a really good um you know, nose for us in the past and when he went to Detroit and back here now, uh I think Baron and Sweaty and me and all the other guys that play edge uh have unique ways that they do certain things. And uh so definitely if you can get it from your upfront, it may not be the same guy over and over again, but that's definitely, you know, it's hard to say right now just one particular guy. I think everyone's done their fair share of um increasingly getting better with their technique and changing the math in certain situations. >> Thursday was the first time in over 200 days that Mack was back on the field from his injury last year. I know it was just a handful of >> Mack? >> Mack Wilson, yeah. He just got hurt last year. >> Mhm. >> And I know it was just a handful of preseason snaps, but sharing the field with him in the green dot, what did you remember about what he brings? >> Oh yeah. Yeah, you know, Mack was super excited. He um he uh definitely has a certain mindset in the way that he plays the game and you know, he's very physical. He's a awesome teammate to have. It's [snorts] really nice, you know, to be out there with him and be able to play with him again, you know, in the same light of that of someone not being out there for a long time as Star. You know, I know Star was pretty emotional about being able to play again. And you see guys, that's the stuff you kind of see behind the scenes is you see guys work their tail off to try and get back and grind and grind and grind. Like I'm talking about guys, you know, we have a kind of a crappy schedule as far as just being in football. It's, you know, it's sunup sundown sometimes, but those guys that are injured, they're there before us and they leave after us doing treatment all year trying to get back just to be able to play on the field again. So, definitely being able to see those guys go out and play again is a huge huge like wholesome moment for everyone, I think. >> We talked to, you know, Coach Fitz about, you know, having a guy like Kendrick run the offense. Do you think it helped, you know, the offensive players that are kind of getting used to a new system? You guys have Nick back. How big of an advantage is that or a comfort level is that to know you have the same coordinator from >> Oh, yeah, it's huge, you know, cuz there's certain things that certain dynamics we went over, especially early on in OTAs and in training camp of what we wanted to change, how we wanted to play certain things, take less, you know, take this much away, add over here. And he's definitely made it a little bit more streamlined for everyone on the the defensive side. Having Nick back is huge thing cuz we know how he thinks, we know how he operates. A lot of guys don't have to learn a new system, you know, you have vets that are that have been in the system that can help the young guys on certain things. So, that's a big kind of stepping stone that you don't really have to go over super early on in OTAs, whereas if you have someone, you know, in any situation, if you have someone new, you have to learn everything from the basics, from language all the way to technique to just how they want to play. >> Between PK and TA though, you guys have had a lot of experience to this defensive coaching staff, right? Not necessarily your room, but what what do you think the benefits are of adding coaches who have that much experience? >> Oh, yeah, for sure, you know, PK being with the D-line and all the experience that he has. And then, you know, so much like TA is awesome. I love TA. We talk quite a bit about football and he's he bounces around room to room and kind of gives his insight on what he thinks and stuff like that. So, he's been very, you know, helpful for I think every position um group so far. You know, that experience of, you know, hey, sometimes think you let things get to you and they become too much or too little and he kind of helps you along the way of, you know, hey, this is kind of a bigger issue and that's, you know, that you kind of just messed up on that player. You just probably thinking this. You know, he's kind of the calm voice where as some other people are yelling at you or something. So, he's kind of he's actually a really good coach. I I like TA a lot. >> You're in your fourth season at outside linebacker starting off ball. How do you think that's kind of transformed your career making that tweak? >> Uh you know, I think about it sometimes. I think you know, getting drafted as a on ball guy or off the ball guy and then switching to on ball. Obviously, there's some learning curves in there for sure. Run defense is run defense but definitely rushing the passer that's a whole that was one of the things early on for sure is like that's a whole new animal for me. I rushed the rushed a little bit early on in my career but not as much as obviously as I do now. Um but it has helped me coming from off the ball understand like conceptually like whenever they're you know, we're in like a base personnel. We have a lot bigger people on the field and I have to guard a slot. You know, it's actually made that job for me a little bit easier coming from that coverage background and that standpoint or even you know, a little bit more passing tight ends in those situations. Whereas, you know, some guys that don't have never dropped before have never really dropped in their career have to get out there and do it. Um Yeah, there have been some dynamics of of learning and wondering if things were other ways but you know, I'm happy where I'm at and with what I've done. Um obviously, we just want to keep climbing the ladder and get better every day.

title: Michael Wilson Press Conference 8.16.26 | AZ Cardinals
text: pretty business like for the starters on uh Saturday night. How do you think it went? >> Uh I thought it was as realistic of a drive that we could have at, you know, this point in training camp and preseason. Had some false starts which we don't like. Um got a bunch of different, you know, third down and distances between like third and five when we threw the the fade ball from the slot tomorrow. Got a PI which can happen. Then we went back to third and 11. And that's when my call to play for me when I ran the the out route from the boundary. Um thought we ran the ball well, blocked well, and then we had the, you know, Mars touchdown. Like what a throw and catch by both those two guys. So it was fun. Everyone touched the ball. Like had a lot of fun out there. >> With uh with where you guys are in the preseason, I mean it seems like you guys are enjoying yourselves. Of course you have a coach come in here and say it's just the preseason. We haven't done anything yet. It's dayto-day. Like how do you kind of balance those two things? You want to keep the optimism at the same time. >> Yeah, I mean obviously Mike's had our coach said a good point before the game. He said like sure preseason games don't count but it does matter. And so um you know anytime you step on any NFL field, whether that be practice, walk through, preseason game, game, everything is you know evaluated to the highest degree possible. And so not only are you are we representing the Cardinals, we're also representing ourselves. And then the the other 31 teams are like scouring the tape. And anytime I step on the field like you never want to put bad stuff on tape at regardless of what it is. And so um I treated you know my preparation for that game was just like a regular game. Like I got out there did worked on my pregame catch routine warmed up make sure I was lubed up ready to go. So it like everything matters to myself and I know our receiver room between KB Marv 3K semi like we got guys who are wired the right way here and here and so like I said everything everything matters. It all it all counts. >> Coach was just saying that he has a soft spot for wide receivers considering his background. Can you sense that he might have a little bit of a soft spot or extra investment in you guys in that receiver room? >> Oh for sure. Yeah, he he knows he knows a lot about a lot about the position. um just like the small details of staying grounded when you catch the football. Um stance and start demeanor pre- snap, post, like he he's got a critical eye for that for that position and you could tell even in team meetings like most head coaches I've been won't won't call out receivers on on certain things and he everything catches his eye which is good. I like it. I like having a coach that's hyper critical about everything because the NFL game is is if you're not on your P's and Q's like you'll get exposed quick. So, it's good to have a coach that that cares about us and is able to evaluate us at the highest degree. >> Your thoughts on on the rookie Jeremiah Love, what he can do, what he brings to the table that can kind of open things up for that wide receiver as well. >> Oh man, it was I mean, I'm sure you guys I saw definitely online was blowing up about it. Um, he's looked like that in practice. Now, I had it's hard to evaluate a running back, I guess, get a full gauge of like what they're fully capable of um during training camp because, you know, there's not that third element where they're getting tackled. And I think for him, like contact balance just he just seems so natural with the ball. I I said this in the interview during the game, but he was he's probably the most natural ball carrier that I've seen with my own two eyes. It's just like he can cut off any foot at any time, spin move. Um, it was it was really special to watch and that's probably the worst he's ever going to look in his career is that game. So, if that's the worst he's ever going to look in his career, that's pretty dang good for us. >> It seems like he's a pretty sharp route runner as well. Does he ever come to you guys for for kind of advice on on that kind of stuff that would you ever work with him? >> Uh, yeah. No, not really. Um, but he does have a natural feel. Like I said, able to cut off any foot. probably one of the best option runners I've ever seen like from a running back to a receiver standpoint just because of his suddenness and his ability to put his foot in the ground and change direction. But and he also has really good hands for running back like the little things about staying grounded, catching the ball with your hands, um catch to transition, like he does all that really well. Probably better than not all receivers in the league, but on par with with some receivers. So, uh, there's really not a thing you can do to be honest. It's it's pretty exciting to watch. >> It's preseason type thing. >> Um, your quarterbacks are like 50 for 59. Yeah. Doesn't matter who's been back there. Doesn't matter who's been catching the ball. Like, >> is >> how much of that do you totally buy into and how much of that is like we got to see what it looks like in regular season? >> For sure. Definitely. I think there's the element of we got to see what it looks like in in regular season, but I mean I'm I've never been a part of a team in preseason that's had those type of numbers. And I'd actually like to see like what the historical data on that is between two games. I mean, we're 15 to 15 uh in the first half between Gardner and Jacobe. And yeah, it seems like it's almost like plug and play. like who's ever out there at wide out who's ever out that out there at uh quarterback it's like regardless it it's it looks the same which is to me what that comes down to I think that's that's a lot is of that is coaching like it's player is executing but it's also getting the right calls in the way that Mike and the offensive staff is detailing things up in the pass game um getting guys open getting guys advantageous one-on- ones um and then from there quarterbacks making the throws and and receivers getting open, but a lot of that is scheme and just, you know, putting players in the right position to to be successful. >> Michael, when you leave the game, you know, after your limited reps, I noticed you in the paint a few times watching the the next wave in there. Yeah, >> that next wave has quite a few playmakers. Yeah, I mean, look at that battle for that back end of the wide receiver. What do you see at this point? There's a lot of a lot of good >> Great question. Yeah, it's a phenomenal room and um you know that how that how those guys are playing in the preseason game like they've been doing that since practice one of OTAAS and so there hasn't been a play that anyone has made in the room from myself all the way down to Trey Wallace that we haven't seen in practice and so like when Reggie goes out and makes a one-handed catch I've seen it before when 3K has 91 yards in the first game 99 90 90 99 yards in the first game, then go six for six for like 52 yards. He's been doing that since day one. He's probably had the best statistically of any receiver in our room from uh charting back all the way to OTAAS in terms of explosives, touchdowns, just like targets to catch ratio. And so, um, and then Simei, like Simey's might be one of the greatest preseason receivers of all time at this point, right? like he just seems every time his number calls he seems to always come through and so it's uh it's a really fun room to be a part of. Um, my favorite part not only is like our onfield play is great, but it's really the off-field character that we have and I just like I said I I said this back in OTAAS, but genuinely excited coming to work every day. Um, not only because of the coaching staff, but more importantly because of the brotherhood that we have in our receiver room because often times that as you guys know it can be a diva position. Everyone that plays receiver is slightly self-interested and so it's great to have a lot of guys that are able to sort of, you know, submit their ego and defeat that ego and it's about like it's about us and our team and our play. >> Speaking that wide receiver room and a guy who's obviously very much not a diva, what have you seen from Marv in this camp? And um I guess where do you feel like he's at in year three in some areas where he's grown? Yeah, I think one thing that I've noticed I think I'd probably noticed this maybe a week or two ago, uh Mar seems a lot I'm not going to say happier. He's he's a happy person, but regardless of result, I've I've really liked how his process has been the same. Um whether he's caught five balls or no balls or one ball in practice, like he's smiling. I'm sure you saw the the play when uh Sime and 3K scored a touchdown. like Marvel was one of the first ones there with a big smile on his face after he caught the touchdown. Big smile on his face. So, it's just good to see Marv smiling a lot. Um because, you know, when his energy is right and his attitude is right, I'm going to keep saying it. You know, he's one of the best receivers in the NFL from a talent perspective. And so, um it's good to see him smiling and having fun playing football because at the end of the day, football is a fun sport and we've all been playing. I've been playing since I was eight years old. And the reason why I still love to play because it's fun at the end of the day. It's it's fun. >> Your role in this offense seems fairly complex, you know, with a lot of motion. You're lining up in all sorts of different spots. What was the adjustment like to kind of all the things that you're asked to do in this offense? And was that a challenge during installs or did it all come naturally? >> It's a great question. Um, definitely a little bit of an adjustment. I think my role is is slightly probably not slight, it's vastly different than say like the back half of the eight games that I played last year cuz last year when Marvin went out I was playing like traditional X receiver, you know, a lot of 3x ones I'm in single coverage like away from the I know Mike has used a term like the Z receiver in offense like tight to the core. A lot of my catches last year were like 3x1 exceiver, fade ball, you know, inside release, bench route, slants, those type of things. And while this offense, like I am still going to be in position to do that, I'm tighter to the core, asked to do a lot more in the run game, which is going to be a big ass for me, but nothing that I am not going to I'm relishing the opportunity to do that because it's also going to give me more opportunities in the pass game. But I think Mike's not asking me to do anything that's not within my skill set and what I was drafted here to do, which is run great routes, catch the football, block really hard. And so I'm doing all those things in this offense. And I think I'm going to excel at those things. And um my goal is to pick up where I left off last year, which is, you know, to produce at a at a top 10 level in the NFL. >> How can you be better prepared to be asked more in I in the run game? >> Uh I think it just starts in practice, right? like what better person to get me ready than Buddha Baker who's, you know, going to be a Hall of Fame safety and then we've got other great guys in that room who are physical in the run game. So, um it's really just when those when I when I do have those reps in practice, there's an element of like you kind of can't go full speed because those are my brothers and my teammates and you know, I don't want to get anyone on our team hurt. But, you know, when it's time to go, like we got to make that block, you know. But, um, so just just the reps in practice, that's really Yeah. is reps in practice.

title: Mike LaFleur Press Conference8.16.26 | AZ Cardinals
text: Jeremiah, have you guys gotten a diagnosis? Do you know if that's a high ankle sprain for sure? >> Uh, it's an ankle. So, we'll keep it at that. >> Coach, you played against this Cardinals defense a lot and you've talked about the the praise you have for it. With the way that Zaven Collins is used, what sort of makes his versatility a unique thing that you guys could try to capitalize on? >> Yeah, well, it's what you just said, the versatility. That's what's kind of always stuck out with him. Um, you know, and it's it's that fine line, too, like and and him and I have had these conversations. Nick and and and him and I had the conversations. Us three had the conversation organically on the field the other day of like utilizing the versatility that he has, that he can play off the ball. He can, you know, be a hot three player in some of the fire zones. Like I don't people don't like seeing outside linebackers in those spots, but every all 32 defenses have something like that, you know, you just don't want to get caught. And sometimes you do get caught and you tip the hat that, hey, wrong call at the wrong time. But, with that being said, because he is versatile doesn't mean he needs to throw all seven pitches every week. Uh, you know, he has a fastball. And that fastball is playing on the edge, you know, in in the run pass game, what whatever have you. So, you know, I think it's our job to make sure that, hey, utilize that versatility, but also, you know, don't thin them out with um just because he is capable of doing some of the stuff that maybe other outside linebackers uh can't. >> Carson was back out there. Didn't look like he was taking any reps in the open portion. Is is this just a day-by-day >> It's yeah, it's a day-by-day. It's um, you know, I full transparency, like the discomfort's still just kind of there, you know, and so um just wanting to let him heal uh a little bit more and um you know, when we're ready to go, we're ready to go. It's not going to be long-term, like I said, but uh you know, that's where we're at. >> When it comes to Jeremiah, I know you kind of touched on it where you see his intensity and even in practice and so, but now that you see it in a game and you kind of see how you could utilize him more or your creative juices flowing or your excitement up there where you're like, man, I can do this with them, or do that with them." >> Yeah, what was cool was I've said it from practice, too. Like, he's a he's a quick learner. Like, in in in a lot of it's you give credit coach Merritt and and you know, some of those like James Conner really helping him out, but like you could see it in the game, too, in terms of from the first drive. I mean, we only had the three drives, but to the third drive in terms of him just staying a little bit more grounded, kind of getting into a little bit of rhythm right there. Um you know, and I like I said, I mean, he he had a good time and and really for him his confidence level went through the roof after that third drive and it's just unfortunate that on the last play it's you know, he gets somewhat rolled up on. >> You don't often see starters or starting running backs getting 14 touches in a preseason game. What did you guys have in mind to accomplish in kind of getting him that that heavy workload during the preseason? >> Yeah, I mean, it's it's a rookie that hadn't played knowing that, you know, not to share too many secrets cuz I haven't said it with the players yet, but knowing that it was about what what it was going to be in terms of how many games these guys were going to play for what we're looking for. So, yeah, that that's what the thought was. >> You've spoken about for Marvin, one of the focuses with him that they can kind of unlock his successes just getting on an edge and really kind of bursting off line of scrimmage. That seems like from the outside like, all right, simple thing to do, right? But I'm sure it's not. I'm sure it's much more complicated than it seems. Why is that more complex than it seems? Like, I'm just run out off line of scrimmage. >> Um well, again, I wasn't here in the past, so I don't really know and I don't really care, but just the constant I wouldn't say demand, but the constant just reminder about how important each blade of grass is. He's he's super talented as you guys know and uh but then you get to this next level and and you know, you want to find every little margin. You want to find just every little inch that you can get to give these guys and we thought, man, he yeah, he gets off the ball fine, but man, he can do it better. And if he does it better, that's just going to unlock different, um, avenues of his game and get him to space a little bit faster because again, it's just inches and inches are milliseconds and milliseconds are everything in this game when there's 22 variables plus referees out on every single snap. So, that's just one area. I mean, you're you're always looking for in in in all these guys, um, different areas to improve and that was one that that stuck out with It wasn't terrible by any means, but it could improve. And, uh, you know, and I think of a guy like Robert Woods. Robert Woods, I thought had the best ball get off, you know, for a few years that that may maybe I don't want to say in the league, but certainly for someone that I watched a lot who was with the Rams when I was with the Niners and that always stuck out because, I mean, that body lean was real and it was every single time and it didn't matter if it was a 6-yard route, 16-yard route, or a vertical route down the field. And so, uh, you know, him, um, really buying into that and and knowing how those little inches are going to help his game, um, I think it's, uh, just helped build his confidence as well. >> Given your background as as working with that position, do you work with that group closer than you do in others during practice? Are you are you over there with it with that group a lot? >> I have a soft spot for receivers and by and by soft spot, I mean, I I uh, tend not to let anything slide with those guys. So, um, they know that and if if they don't, Kendrick lets them know that, um, from my time with them. So, um, yeah, I mean, it's I I'm with them naturally, you know, you you let your position coaches coach and and you I mean, part of my job was trying to hire the best staff that I possibly could, uh, and trust the guys to do what they do and, uh, and and pour into it because I've also, you know, seen it where, um, a coordinator head coach tries to do everything and now it kind of dilutes the position coach a little and that's never what I want to do. With that being said, I'm I'm certainly around the offense a lot. I think the the the play caller needs to be around the offense a lot, a little bit more around the skill than the O line because of time on task value received, making sure that they have their time and not hearing stuff that's just not important, but at sometimes I do want them to hear what I'm telling the receivers just so there's a shared accountability there. Just like you want the receivers to hear what we're telling the offensive line to give and take right there. So, yeah, I mean they they they hear from me, they hear from Hack, they hear from Tony. Um Justin Fry did a presentation for the group today on quarterback sneak. You wouldn't believe how long this thing went. But it was necessary. But it But it was necessary cuz it was extremely detailed and it was a honestly the best quarterback sneak presentation I'd ever heard. And it was juice and there was you know, it was real. And he had passion for it, you know, so I know I'm going on a little rant right there, but yeah, so I'm I'm around those guys. >> You mentioned James Conner helping out Jeremiah. What what areas have you seen that really take hold? >> You know, it it's it's more of what I hear. Backs in general are usually the ones that are for whatever reason the quietest ones of the unit. They just kind of all hang out and do their thing right there and you know, but then when they go into their meeting rooms obviously coach Merritt's doing the talking holding the clicker, but when you have a guy like James you're going to utilize that that asset, that resource. And so just just hearing about what's going on in there, you know, hearing about just after the game, even during the game some of the things that James was talking to Jeremiah. And I thought you could see it, you know, from from first drive to the third drive. And uh you know, so just just pleased with with you know, what James does for that group. >> How does it And how and how can it help you to have Born in in the room cuz he he's your guy, right? He knows you as well as any other coach. >> my guys. I just know them more. >> Okay, you know them longer, but how how's it help having a guy like that who kind of knows how you're thinking, what you're thinking? >> You know, that's really has nothing to do with why he's here. He's here because one I think he can help the Arizona Cardinals win football games and move the ball down the field. Um and two, he brings great energy. Now, because I was with him for 4 years, I I understood that and that is infectious. Like just the meeting rooms, the the practice field, like it's the same every single day day. There's no highs and low. He just lives in the high like all the time. But that's that's that's his standard. That's his norm and um I've seen it firsthand where he's affected other people because the energy he brings. And so, um again, hey first and foremost, can he help us move the ball forward? Is he exactly what we want from a you know, the way he practice standard? Absolutely. And then the the the second part was, like I said, the energy. Knowing that that's just going to uplift other guys. >> You said yesterday and you know, you pointed asked about Walter and you had you know, pointed to his explosiveness, but you also said there there are things that he's still working on. You know, he has ways to go. What are the things that he's still What can he still improve as a player? Because watching him, like the explosiveness is so obvious, but I'm sure there's other things that are less obvious that that you still want him to work on. >> Yeah, no, that's it's a good question and it's it to me it's it's not even to go too detailed with it, it's time on task value received. Um when he was playing last year, uh albeit minimal, he affected the game in all phases, run game and and and pass game and we saw that. I've been on record and I told him this yesterday and the truth is, when we studied the Arizona Cardinals last year, um when Walt was out there compared to when he wasn't was a different tape at times. And we knew going into both those games that Walt wasn't playing, so you could almost disregard that. There was a respect that we had for him in terms of the player. Uh but he wasn't out there a ton uh for obvious reasons and some of it there a lot of it was uncontrollable. He can't control some of those factors. So, you know, now that he is able to practice and he is feeling healthy and he's he's getting his confidence, it's hey, every single snap, every single snap we got to go and cuz you have the ability to affect the game. Uh and when you affect the game, it makes the people behind you's job a lot easier. Not just the corners that are having to cover receivers on the perimeter, but the linebackers, all those kind of things and so he he has it in him to go do that. Again, time on task, value received for for what he's going to do. I really like Walt. Walt can be as good as he wants to be. I know that. I know his teammates know that and and Walt's a good person and now it's just about stacking those days. >> Find yourself getting any more comfortable calling plays in Vegas compared to camp? >> Yeah, cuz it's I mean, it's the preseason. Like it's they're not the defense isn't doing anything, we're not doing anything. It's you know, you're just trying to go operate and stuff like that. So I can't say I if anything it was probably harder in Vegas cuz I had no clue what that coordinator was going to do. So we were just going to kind of wing it after the first few drives and and go. Like I'll be honest, I didn't look at the call sheet until like two hours before the game, you know, and uh because you're again, you're just running protected plays and and I you know, I I didn't know what they were going to do. So you try to run the stuff that our guys are confident in doing and you know, solving their own problems. I know Fro said it yesterday like, you know, we had a play in the first drive, first and 10, we ran into what we call a 55 front where there's a three, a six eye and then an overhang Sam backer and we're running our wide zone right into it. Like it's not a good play. Like it can draw up okay, but it's like it's a numbers game, right? Like where they have people, they are covering space, run away from that, right? I mean, it's pretty simple in terms of some of that stuff. You know, but hey, there's might be a time where like, hey, we don't want to put a can on it. Let's just go play and then we get caught in a 55 front. Hey guys, we we're able to coach off of that and it's not the end of the world. Don't love it, you know, we'll we'll regather and get back in the huddle and play the second play. So yeah, I mean, that's that's kind of how I feel. >> With Walt, he said that he cleaned up his diet this off season cut about 10 pounds. You mentioned being able to go 100% every play. Do you think that that can kind of help him be be to go 100%? >> Yeah, I mean, just based off of what he has said to to I think you guys and to to me and stuff like that. So, again, I don't I didn't know what he weighed last year cuz again, I wasn't here. I didn't see what he looked like in practice, all that. All I saw was those minimal amount of games in the game tape and and the disruption that uh he he caused. So, but you know, if the 10 lbs are is a good weight loss for him and he feels more explosive and more powerful and all those kind of things, great. It's like I think I told you guys like I don't know what the ideal weight is for all these guys. [snorts] Like you have to communicate with them. Like do you feel good? Certainly, there's guys that are lighter than they should be. Certainly, there's guys that look like they're probably heavier than they should be. But like when you start talking about the margins, you gain five, lose five, all that kind of stuff, it's like what can he be to be the most explosive dominant athlete that he can be? And and that's a discussion amongst people that are smarter than me, nutritionists, strength coaches, all those kind of things, but also the the player. And and you have to collectively come to an agreement or somewhat of an agreement in terms of you know, where you want it. So. >> Coach, we'll make this the last one. When you install a new offense in a new place like you are here, what's the biggest challenge in that and how has the offense kind of been received by the players in terms of like getting it down, understanding those >> Yeah, you know, I mean, anytime it's it's like a a foreign language initially and that's everywhere you've been. Even if even with guys like Jacob um how about even Kendrick Bourne? Like what they did in in San Francisco when he got back there's different than what he was doing when we were there in 20 and it's different than what we're doing here in Arizona. So, there's a natural learning curve in in terms of what we're trying to get done. But again, I look at it, hey, you're just trying to stack days and and you know, they're going to get sick of me with this, but like again, I don't assume that they they remember or know anything. I want to coach it every single day with the the of time that we have allotted uh you know, to the to the highest degree of of detail, uh so that they can go out and not think and then just go do the things that they can do that we as coaches can't.
